science.title: Wild bee Lasioglossum malachurum (Hymenoptera: Halictidae) responses to pesticides and urban pollutants: linking cholinesterase activity and morphological traits
science.description: Wild bees are important pollinators. However, their populations are threatened by pesticide exposure and urban pollution. This study examines the effects of environmental pollutants on the wild bee species Lasioglossum malachurum. Cholinesterase (ChE) activity and protein levels were measured as physiological biomarkers, while morphological traits (weights and ratios) were evaluated as alternative anatomical biomarkers of neurotoxicity. Bees were sampled from organic agriculture (reference site), conventional agriculture (pesticide exposure), and urban agriculture (urban pollution). Significant declines in ChE activity and protein content were observed in bees from conventionally managed fields, suggesting pesticide-induced neurotoxicity and impaired protein assimilation. Moreover, morphological alterations, particularly a substantial decrease in both head-to-total and head-to-body ratios, were found to be associated with acetylcholinesterase inhibition. Conversely, bees from urban agriculture exhibited increased body protein content and ChE activity but no significant morphological alterations, indicating an adaptive response to sublethal urban pollutants. Overall, morphological biomarkers showed promise as rapid and practical anatomical indicators of neurotoxicity from pesticide exposure, in accordance with findings of physiological biomarkers. However, their effectiveness was limited in urban environments due to the complexity of urban pollutants. This study highlights the importance of integrating physiological and morphological biomarkers into biomonitoring frameworks, contributing to the development of non-destructive methodologies.
